1.
INTRODUCTION
This staff working document (SWD) reports on the interim evaluation of the Fiscalis programme
(hereafter: ‘the programme’). The programme is one of the principal tools used to support the
implementation of European Union taxation policy. The programme provides a framework for
improving the functioning of the taxation systems in the single market by increasing cooperation
between participating countries, their tax authorities and officials. By ensuring the exchange of
information, supporting administrative cooperation and increasing participating countries’
administrative capacity, the programme supports: (i) the implementation of EU law in the field of
taxation; and (ii) the fight against tax fraud, tax evasion and aggressive tax planning. The programme's
main beneficiaries are the EU Member States' tax administrations and its budget of EUR 269 million
for the period 2021-2027 supports three main types of activities, namely: (i) EESs, which have
accounted for over 80% of the budget so far; (ii) actions fostering collaboration among tax
administrations; and (iii) capacity-building actions.
The Fiscalis programme was set up by Regulation (EU) No 2021/847 of the European Parliament and
of the Council of 20 May 2021 establishing an action programme to improve the operation of taxation
systems in the European Union. In line with Article 15(2) of the Regulation establishing the
programme, the Commission must carry out an interim evaluation no later than four years after the
implementation of the programme is launched and must communicate the conclusions of the interim
[…and final] evaluations, including its observations, to the European Parliament, the Council, the
European Economic and Social Committee and to the Committee of the Regions.
1.1 Purpose and scope of the evaluation
Building on previous assessments, this evaluation focuses on the common components of the EESs
in the area of taxation, which account for most of the total budget allocated to the Fiscalis programme.
To a certain but lesser extent, the evaluation also covers the programme’s other core activities,
namely: (i) collaborative actions (which provide a platform for tax officials and other stakeholders to
cooperate and ensure, for example, uniform implementation of EU tax law); (ii) expert teams (a
relatively new bottom-up activity allowing the Member States to jointly develop specific initiatives);
and (iii) human capacity building. Since most of these activities were evaluated previously and have
been relatively stable over the years, the evaluation focuses on aspects that have recently been
introduced or have undergone recent changes. In this vein, when it comes to collaborative activities,
the evaluation also assesses the programme’s new monitoring and evaluation framework (MEF) and
takes into consideration follow-up measures arising from the evaluation of the previous iteration of
the programme.
The purpose of the evaluation is to assess the Fiscalis programme’s progress towards its main
objectives between 2021 and 2024, in terms of the five better regulation criteria of effectiveness,
efficiency (with a focus on costs and benefits), coherence, relevance and EU added value1.
1 This evaluation follows and fulfils the Commission’s better regulation requirements as updated in July 2023. See ‘Better
regulation’ guidelines (2021) and toolbox (2023): Better regulation: guidelines and toolbox.
4
Under the overall criterion of effectiveness, the evaluation examines first to what extent the Fiscalis
programme has been successful over the relevant period, and then, the possible reasons behind that.
The evaluation does this by focusing on the implementation and achievements of the different types
of activities and their relative contribution to the programme’s objectives. The efficiency of the
Fiscalis programme is evaluated by looking at the costs and benefits of the EESs and their
components, and the administrative burden for tax authorities and economic operators. The evaluation
then investigates the efficiency of the non-EES components, including training activities,
collaborative actions, the learning management system/platform, e-learning, and common learning
events. At this stage (i.e. halfway through the funding period) this will shed light on the extent to
which the programme’s budget (EUR 269 million between 2021 and 2027) has been spent efficiently
on the activities that it supports. The analysis also looks at the efficiency of the overall programme
management and governance.
The assessment of relevance covers two main aspects, namely: (i) the alignment of the programme’s
objectives with the EU's needs and challenges in the field of taxation; and (ii) the appropriateness and
fitness for purpose of the programme's features and set-up, specifically as regards its support for the
common components of the EESs and for collaborative activities, training and other actions. The
analysis of coherence will look at the extent to which the programme is coherent with other EU
initiatives/programmes with similar objectives, and at the internal consistency of the actions funded
by the programme itself. Thus, the evaluation will report on the implementation of the
recommendations regarding the Fiscalis programme's consistency with the Union anti-fraud
programme2, and its alignment with measures such as the instrument for pre-accession assistance
(IPA) and the instrument for technical assistance and information exchange (TAIEX) among others.
Lastly, the evaluation will examine the criterion of EU added value to report on the extent to which
the programme has brought about changes beyond those which could have been expected as a result
of national actions by the Member States acting alone. This aspect is assessed by looking at both the
EU added value of the different types of activities funded by the programme (i.e. IT systems, the
Customs & Tax EU Learning Portal, expert teams and collaborative actions) and the programme's
overall added value.
The overall evaluation methodology3 consisted of three main phases: (i) a structuring phase, which
included preparatory activities for designing and developing the evaluation, such as selecting an
external contractor and identifying relevant stakeholders to be consulted; (ii) data collection and
analysis, involving stakeholder consultations, legal and desk research, and analytical work to support
the assessment; and (iii) evaluation and insights, where the information collected was analysed to
produce the evaluation report by examining the five better regulation criteria and subsequently
drawing conclusions and lessons learned.
This evaluation is primarily based on the findings of an external study carried out over a 12-month
period by a consortium led by Economisti Associati4. In order to devise a suitable approach to the
evaluation, some critical elements had to be accounted for at the outset of the exercise. These

developed and improved over time, while remaining broadly stable; (ii) the budgetary split, whereby
most of the programme's resources are devoted to a number of IT systems (EESs) in the field of
taxation; (iii) the fact that collaborative activities and human capacity-building actions have already
been extensively evaluated; (iv) the difficulties faced by previous evaluations, particularly in
measuring the IT systems' costs and benefits, and dealing with ‘consultation fatigue’ among core
stakeholders; and (v) the recent launch of the MEF, which provides a more solid base for monitoring
data than has been available for past evaluations. This led to an approach that relies heavily on case
studies to investigate as deeply as possible the issues that are of most interest, while dedicating less
time and effort to assessing all the programme’s components (since previous evaluations have
covered this quite exhaustively)5.
Data for both the case studies and the programme-level assessment was collected via three main
methods: (i) desk research to review a wide range of relevant sources of secondary data and
information; (ii) 84 interviews with representatives of national tax authorities, economic operators
and the European Commission; and (iii) three separate targeted surveys, namely one for NFCs in
the national tax authorities of participating countries (27 respondents), and two short online user
surveys as part of two of the case studies (on VIES-on-the-web (1 248 respondents) and the LMS (62
respondents)).

2.
WHAT WAS THE EXPECTED OUTCOME OF THE INTERVENTION?
The predecessor to the current Fiscalis programme (Fiscalis 2020) ran from 2014 to 2020. The
findings of the final evaluation, published in 2022, indicate that the programme was broadly
successful in achieving its objectives6. The evaluation recognised that some limitations had affected
the analysis, but concluded that Fiscalis 2020 had delivered efficient and effective results for tax
authorities and businesses. There are examples that illustrate that specific activities carried out under
Fiscalis 2020, such as data sharing through the DAC1 and DAC2 systems, simplified both
communication between authorities and compliance with tax rules. Feedback gathered through
consultations also indicated that Fiscalis 2020 activities were perceived as useful by key stakeholders
and as having had an impact on their organisations’ working practices7. Specific initiatives also
provided evidence of the programme's value added, such as the development of the TNA system and
the excise duty calculator, which ‘might not have existed if Fiscalis 2020 did not provide funding for
expert teams’8.
2.1 Description of the intervention and its objectives
The current Fiscalis programme (for 2021-2027) aligns with the original objective of improving
cooperation among tax authorities. In the proposal for the 2021-2027 Fiscalis programme, the
Commission recognised the successes of previous Fiscalis programmes, while acknowledging that
more progress should be made in fostering cooperation among tax authorities9. The resulting
Regulation (adopted by the Council and the Parliament following the agreement on the MFF for 2021-
2027) allocates EUR 269 million in current prices to the Fiscalis programme, up from EUR 223.2
million in the 2014-2020 period10. In addition to the EU Member States, participation in the
programme (and in
some but not all of its activities and IT systems) is open to candidate and potential candidate countries,
with a view both to fostering convergence and supporting the programme's objectives.
The intervention logic of the programme hinges on three general objectives, namely:
• supporting tax authorities and taxation in order to improve the functioning of the internal
market;
• fostering the competitiveness of the EU and fair competition in the EU; and
• protecting (including from tax fraud, tax evasion and tax avoidance) the financial and
economic interests of the EU and its Member States.
In turn, these general objectives are reflected in three specific objectives, which comprise:

The activities of the Fiscalis programme are categorised in three main areas.
• EESs received 84% of the Fiscalis budget between 2021 and 202411 for developing,
maintaining and improving EESs to boost coordination and information sharing. The primary
aim of the EESs is to help implement EU tax legislation properly and to support tax authorities
in performing their tasks.
• Collaboration actions, including expert teams, provide a platform for tax authorities to
share their knowledge, experience and good practices, and to jointly develop operational
guidelines. This is achieved by supporting the setting up of meetings and project-based
collaboration. In most cases, the support consists of costs for travel, accommodation and
subsistence, while salary costs can also be covered for certain actions.
• Capacity building and human competency aims to improve performance across EU tax
authorities. Fiscalis supports capacity building through e-learning, workshops and training
sessions, ensuring that tax officials are equipped to manage modern taxation challenges. This
includes the development of a dedicated online portal, the Customs & Tax EU Learning
Portal12.

Several inputs underpin these activities, including financial resources (i.e. the programme budget)
that are used to: (i) obtain (primarily IT-related) services via public procurement; and (ii) provide
grants to enable stakeholders (mainly national tax administrations) to participate in the activities.
Human resources from both the European Commission and national levels are essential. The
multiannual work programmes (MAWP) (of which two have been produced so far, and the
multiannual strategic planning for taxation (MASP-T) provide direction for the programme.
While the form of the programme has been broadly stable across funding periods, the current
programme has some new features. The first new feature concerns the introduction of the MASP-T,
which sets out a strategic framework and milestones for managing the IT projects funded by the
programme13. Another new feature is the way in which collaborative activities are managed, with the
Commission no longer disbursing funding directly, but now awarding grants to a consortium
comprising tax administrations from participating countries. Lastly, dedicated ‘innovation activities’,
such as proof of concept, pilot projects and prototypes, can be funded under the Fiscalis Regulation.
The European Commission (DG TAXUD) is responsible for implementing Fiscalis under direct
management14. The programme is implemented on the basis of programming cycles in the form of
MAWPs, which represent the programme’s operational and financial framework. Two MAWPs (for
2021-2023 and for 2024-2025) have been produced so far. The Commission programme management
team (CPMT), which is part of DG TAXUD, ensures the strategic and overall management of the
Fiscalis programme, as well as providing oversight. The CPMT operates with the help of the Fiscalis
programme committee and national programme coordinators (NPCs) and their teams. The Fiscalis
committee was set up under Article 18 of the Regulation and is composed of delegates from all
participating countries. It plays a formal role in the programme's governance and decision-making
process, particularly concerning the legal endorsement of strategic documents, such as the MAWPs.
In contrast, the NPCs come together in a Commission expert group15, which also forms one of the
programme’s collaborative actions (see description of the actions below). The NPCs are designated
by each participating country and have a more operational function, involving the coordination and
day-to-day implementation of the programme, including the planning and monitoring of actions at
national level. The management arrangements for the different types of actions are as follows.
• For the EESs, DG TAXUD retains coordination functions, and develops and operates the EU
components of the systems, while (where relevant) the Member States develop and operate
national components.
• Collaborative actions are conducted via grant agreements with participating administrations,
represented by a grant coordinator (currently the Latvian tax authority for the collaborative
activities grant). Both the programme beneficiary countries and the Commission can initiate,
chair and lead such collaborative activities. Collaborative activities fall into two broad

2.2. Point(s) of comparison
The first version of the Fiscalis programme was launched in 1998 and has been followed without
interruption by subsequent versions since then. Therefore, it is rather limiting to compare the situation
under the current programme with a hypothetical scenario where no Fiscalis programme exists.
Subsequent versions of the programme have created a baseline of cooperation in the field of taxation
and have evolved gradually to address new and emerging challenges and priorities. Therefore,
comparing the developments in the last few years with the situation before 1998, or imagining a
sudden disappearance of the entire programme would not be overly instructive.
Relevant information that can act as a sort of ‘baseline’ can be draw from the final evaluation of
Fiscalis 202016, which concluded that the programme had been effective in achieving its objectives
and would probably continue to be a relevant tool at EU level for achieving the goals of supporting
the implementation of EU tax legislation and the fight against tax fraud, tax evasion and aggressive
tax planning. The final evaluation of Fiscalis 2020 also identified some areas where there is room for
improvement, such as weak evidence on the costs and benefits of the IT systems, and the need for
non-EU countries to be able to participate in a wider set of activities.
Both assessments provide indications that can be used to: (i) contextualise and compare the
performance of the current programme with that of its predecessor; and (ii) assess to what extent
the conclusions of the previous evaluation continue to be valid, and whether the weaknesses identified
have been effectively addressed.
In addition to this, the following aspects also provide relevant points of comparison.
- An MEF for the current programme has been developed, and DG TAXUD has set targets and
collected data for the relevant indicators since the inception of the programme. Where possible
and appropriate, the evaluation considers how these indicators have developed over time, from
the ‘baseline’ in 2021 until 2024.
- The reliance on in-depth case studies to assess the effectiveness (including the costs and benefits
of selected IT systems) is a key element of the methodology for this evaluation. To facilitate a
robust analysis, each case study developed a counterfactual to consider what would have been

3.
HOW HAS THE SITUATION EVOLVED OVER THE EVALUATION PERIOD?
3.1 Current state of play
The current Fiscalis programme (2021-2027), which has a budget of EUR 269 million reflecting
recent EU policy developments, continues to pursue its original goal of improving cooperation
between tax authorities. The programme's budget supports the expansion and modernisation of IT
systems in the tax area to meet the growing need for more sophisticated digital tools. Guided by the
2021-2023 and 2024-2025 MAWPs, which outline the priorities and actions for each period, the
programme focuses on key components, such as developing and implementing EESs, establishing
expert teams and improving capacity building within tax administrations across the EU.
The MAWPs provide a clear roadmap for the Fiscalis programme by identifying priority actions that
address the changing needs of tax administrations in the context of cross-border cooperation,
digitalisation and tax compliance. Each of the programme’s components is designed to foster
collaboration, improve operational efficiency and build the necessary expertise to meet current and
future tax challenges.
After the Fiscalis 2020 programme, the funding cycle of the current Fiscalis programme began in
2021. However, as part of the transition, unused resources from the Fiscalis 2020 programme,
covering both IT projects and collaborative actions, were implemented in 2021 due to delays in the
adoption of the 2021-2027 MFF and the subsequent late adoption of the Fiscalis Regulation. Training
activities also continued to be funded through the Fiscalis 2020 budget until December 2021.
The budget allocation for the 2021-2024 period is distributed across several key categories, as
outlined in the MAWPs and detailed in Table 1 below. As with previous funding periods, most of the
budget has been committed to the EESs category. For collaboration activities, which include expert
teams, EUR 8.5 million (a large sum due to the fact that grants are multiannual as from 2021
(covering on average 2-3 years)) was allocated in 2021, with EUR 500 000 allocated in 2022. This
amount increased again to about EUR 1 million in 2024.
The ‘other service contracts category’, which covers areas such as training and consultancy, saw an
allocation of EUR 1.2 million in 2022, which increased to EUR 3.8 million in 2024. This expenditure
supports the operational activities, and the various external services needed to support the programme.
In 2021, EUR 70 000 was designated for external experts, but no funds were allocated to this category
subsequently from 2022 to 2024.
Overall, the total committed expenses for the Fiscalis programme have been relatively stable,
increasing gradually from just under EUR 34.5 million in 2021 to EUR 38.4 million in 2024.

Box 1. Overview of the case studies
TNA
•
TNA is a centralised, automated risk analysis platform supporting Eurofisc’s fight against cross-border VAT
fraud, especially missing trader intra-community (MTIC) and carousel fraud (whereby illicit traders claim
repayments for input VAT that was never incurred). The system enables real-time data exchange and network
analysis among national tax authorities for the early detection of fraudsters and fraud facilitators. Operational since
2020, TNA replaced manual Excel-based data exchanges of information, which were time-consuming and affected
by quality issues (e.g. clerical errors in compilations, missing information, different formats). When it was
introduced, TNA covered only MTIC fraud, but its scope was subsequently expanded to include VAT fraud that
involves the violation of customs procedures (2021) and fraud related to means of transportation (2023).
•
Key findings: TNA was found to be highly effective in: (i) detecting VAT fraud; (ii) enabling early warnings;
(iii) improving the targeting of tax controls; and (iv) supporting real-time collaboration between Member States.
Between its introduction in 2020 and 2023, some EUR 37 billion in suspicious transactions were uncovered22,
with over 12 000 fraudsters being identified and 6 000 deregistered for VAT. TNA also achieved significant
success in preventing fraud by identifying fraudsters early and thus reducing their lifespan and, consequently, the
volume of their fraudulent activities. The system also led to significant cost savings for tax authorities (in the
order of EUR 1.7 million by 2024) by automating data collection and processing. Further (likely significant)
savings are generated by streamlining bilateral interactions, which can now be carried out on the system instead
of through lengthy administrative procedures.
DAC 6 Central Directory (CD)
•
The DAC6 CD is a central repository for exchanging information on reportable cross-border arrangements
that might have some tax avoidance consequences, in compliance with the obligation stemming from the fifth
amendment to the Directive on Administrative Cooperation23 (or DAC6). Under DAC6, information is collected
from reporting entities (tax advisers and other intermediaries or, as a last resort, taxpayers) through nationally
developed systems, and then transmitted machine-to-machine to the CD. The process is highly automated and
requires little or no human intervention. Similar processes are used to bulk download information on national
repositories to be used for tax controls and risk assessment by national tax officials.
•
Key findings: the case study suggests that DAC6 CD works well, and stakeholders only pointed out minor issues
or possible improvements. Most tax authorities believe that a centralised system (as opposed to bilateral
exchanges) is the right choice for these types of exchanges, although implementing a centralised system is not
necessarily less costly than bilateral exchanges. Tax authorities largely agree that DAC6 CD has three main
advantages. Firstly, it reduces the costs of follow-ups compared with bilateral interactions. Secondly, it

Vies on-the-web (VoW)
•
VoW is a web interface that is integrated with the VAT information Exchange System (VIES). Launched in
2001, VoW allows economic operators to verify business partners’ VAT numbers. Operating on a real-time
basis, each validation request made through VoW is instantly forwarded to the relevant administration's national
VIES system. If the entered VAT number is valid, the platform confirms its validity. If that is not the case, the
platform notifies users that the VAT number is invalid for cross-border transactions within the EU. Additionally,
it advises economic operators to reach out to the appropriate authorities for corrections or clarifications, providing
a useful link to the national tax authorities for further assistance. Before VoW became operational, the verification
of VAT numbers was cumbersome and varied significantly in different country-specific contexts. The process for
providing VAT details (including the VAT identification number of the buyer and the VAT amount due) was
manual and fragmented, often requiring the consultation of national VAT databases, direct communication with
tax authorities, or contact with trading partners. The launch of VoW marked a significant step towards centralising
and digitising the VAT number verification process, streamlining it for traders.
▪
Key findings: the case study found evidence that VoW has provided economic operators with a rapid, reliable and
centralised system for VAT number verification, dramatically changing the processes and tools available for
business and tax officials to verify VAT numbers. By standardising verification practices, VoW reduces national
disparities in data access and improves operational efficiency for businesses. Its main benefits include a
reduced administrative burden, and better VAT compliance and VAT enforcement. The centralisation of VAT
number verification delivers substantial cost savings, as tax authorities and economic operators would incur
higher costs in the counterfactual scenario. VoW allowed both tax authorities and economic operators to achieve
average cost savings in the order of EUR 62 million between 2021 and 2023, with a cost/benefit ratio of 7.524.
VoW also demonstrates significant EU added value by providing an EU platform for rapid, reliable and
centralised VAT number verification, which ensures interoperability with national VIES systems, brings
consistency and uniformity and lowers costs for tax administrations and businesses. Finally, the VAT in the Digital
Age initiative and the growing adoption of e-invoicing are expected to increase VoW’s capabilities and usage in
the future. The case study also identified significant areas for improvement, including improvements to the user
interface and platform accessibility, adjusting the daily limit on requests and modernising the API interface.
Excise Movement Control System (EMCS)
•
The purpose of the EMCS is to track the movement of excisable goods (alcohol, tobacco and energy products)
throughout the EU. It aims to improve the efficiency, safety, security and environmental footprint of the
monitoring of such goods. The system monitors several key types of information including: (i) the economic
operators; (ii) the consignors (the sender of the excisable good) and consignees (the recipient of the excisable
good), who have to be registered; (iii) the type of excisable good (listed in the EMCS code sheet); (iv) the details
of the provider of the mandatory movement guarantee; and (v) even the details of the transporter. Structurally,
EMCS is a complex, distributed system with both central and Member State components. The Commission is
responsible for developing and maintaining several components, including: (i) the SEED database, a central
registry which is used to automatically verify the validity of every movement against the trader records before the
goods are approved and moved; (ii) the SEED-on-Europa application, a data-searching tool, which allows
economic operators to check the validity of a SEED number in any Member State; and (iii) several other

➢ The programme's actions helped to implement EU tax law uniformly and, thus, to improve
the functioning of the EU single market
Fiscalis support for the common components of the EESs represents an essential element of EU tax
policy and its implementation. Since most of the recent EU tax policies and legislation require a
digital solution, IT capacity building is indispensable for the operationalisation of new initiatives
and actions. This is the case, for instance, for all DAC AEOI provisions. The Directive, in fact,
obliges the Commission to: (i) develop and maintain the central components of the infrastructure and
software necessary for the exchanges, which typically also provide access to horizontal infrastructures
(e.g. CCN/CCN2 and CSI); and/or (ii) develop central systems (e.g. DAC6). As discussed in the
dedicated case study, the IT solution conceived influenced the design of the policy, with the two being
completely intertwined.
In other cases, IT systems have improved and strengthened the implementation of existing or
evolving provisions. For instance, the introduction of the EMCS streamlined and improved the
processes related to the movement of excise goods, allowing the transition from paper-based to
electronic processes to be made. This helped not only to simplify and reduce the administrative
burden on economic operators, but also to strengthen tax authorities’ ability to monitor the
movements, thereby helping to implement the related policy fully.
The role of collaborative actions in implementing EU tax law uniformly is recognised across the
board by the stakeholders consulted, both in individual case studies and in the overall programme
assessment35. Those actions provide forums for national tax officials to exchange best practices,
develop common standards for the implementation of rules or the uptake of IT systems, and share
views and experiences across different legal, institutional and cultural backgrounds, in a way that
would not be possible without the programme.

From an operational viewpoint, collaborative actions contribute to the implementation of EU law in
several different ways, some of which are set out below.
• There are structured activities, such as those carried out by project groups and expert teams
(including the TNA and the CESOP expert teams) that have engaged in the design,
development, roll-out and training of the IT systems funded by the programme. Those
structured activities are complemented by numerous events, such as IT training sessions,
CLEP events, workshops and seminars that aim to build the skills of tax authorities in using
the new or improved systems.
• There are also actions that aim to support uniform implementation through long-lasting
or permanent activities with operational functions. Such actions are carried out by
dedicated project groups, such as the EU Advanced International Administrative Cooperation
(AIAC) community, the standing committee for the implementation of Article 10 of the
Directive on tax dispute resolution mechanisms in the EU, or by the project groups supporting
the implementation of the GloBE minimum tax directive, the VAT OSS and the VAT scheme
for SMEs, as well as numerous workshops and seminars. Within these forums, tax authorities
can exchange best practices to strive for the harmonised implementation of EU tax law and to
ensure the adoption and uptake of the related IT systems.
• Other activities, such as MLCs and PAOEs, focus on compliance and correct
implementation. These activities allow Member States to concentrate on compliance with
the conditions of EU legislation, but they do not necessarily focus on differences between
countries. In a similar vein, most of the training actions, particularly the e-learning modules,
are focused on helping stakeholders to correctly implement or (in the case of economic
operators) comply with EU tax legislation.
Interaction between programme support for EESs and collaborative actions
While both IT systems and collaborative actions contribute to the implementation of EU tax law, and
thus to the functioning of the single market, they do so through different channels. IT systems are
an increasingly integral part of EU tax policies and law (often stemming from a requirement in
EU law) and thus contribute directly to the creation of a level playing field. In this respect, the role
of collaborative actions and learning activities is inextricably connected to the uniform
implementation of tax policies and laws, and to their uptake. This second aspect is essential for the
policies to produce the desired results.

Efficiency
The assessment of the efficiency criterion looks at the programme's benefits in relation to its costs to
determine whether it has been cost-effective. In this regard, the Fiscalis monitoring framework
explicitly mentioned the imperative to foster ‘more efficient tax authorities’ (result 3). The analysis
below looks at the extent to which the programme’s budget (EUR 269 million between 2021 and
2027) has been spent efficiently so far (i.e. halfway through the funding period) on the activities that
it supports.
In line with the broader evaluation approach, the first efficiency-related question focuses on the costs
and benefits of the EESs (and their central components) funded under the Fiscalis programme. To
answer this question, the evaluation will draw mainly on the four IT case studies by highlighting both
the similarities between them, as well as key findings for the individual systems. The following strand
will draw on the LMS case study to investigate the efficiency of the non-EES components, including
training activities, collaborative actions, the LMS, e-learning and common learning events. Lastly,
this section will also deal with the efficiency of overall programme management and governance.

Cost effectiveness of EESs
Comparing the costs and benefits of the four systems assessed in the case studies allows the following
inferences to be made regarding cost effectiveness38:
- For TNA, the time savings compared to the counterfactual scenario can be quantified at
approximately seven staff days per month for each tax administration, resulting in cost savings of
around EUR 1.7 million between 2021 and 2027. This estimate may be reductive, as it does not
take into account, firstly, the amount of time saved by Eurofisc working field coordinators when
managing exchanges of information and aggregating data, which is likely considerable. Secondly,
it does not take into account the savings related to requests for qualification, notifications and
other bilateral interactions. These are now carried out on the TNA directly and would take longer
to carry out by other means, though, as mentioned above, interviewees were not able to quantify
these.
- For VoW, centralising VAT number verification through a platform funded by the Commission
has resulted in significant cost savings. The time savings compared to the counterfactual scenario
(which would entail national systems being made accessible to economic operators from all
Member States) can be quantified at some 120 staff days per month for each administration. This
assumes that each administration would otherwise need to hire four staff members dedicated to
developing and maintaining the platform, and two staff members to manage the helpdesk and
troubleshooting support for VoW users. Across the EU, this translates to approximately 162 full-
time equivalents (FTEs) and total annual salaries of approximately EUR 7 909 24539. This reflects
significant time and resource savings compared to the counterfactual scenario, where
development, maintenance and support costs fall to Member States. Due to the hypothetical nature
of the costs, these estimates involve a significant degree of uncertainty. Nonetheless, they give an
approximate indication of the additional costs that MS authorities might incur in the absence of

resource allocation (human and time), VAT verification costs, batch requests and API integration

Coherence
The external coherence of the Fiscalis programme was assessed positively in previous evaluation
exercises. Looking at the two most recent evaluations, the final evaluation of Fiscalis 2020 found the
programme to be ‘coherent and consistent with EU priorities and complement other funding
programmes’, while the mid-term evaluation found ‘strong evidence of external coherence,
underpinned by the programme’s consistency with the Europe 2020 Strategy (the key policy reference

consistency was hardly surprising, given that the Fiscalis programme exists to support the
development and implementation of EU tax policy, which is itself aligned with other policies and

➢ Other EU policies and interventions have accelerated progress towards the Fiscalis objectives
Over the last decade, the EU has experienced a policy and cultural shift when it comes to tax
fraud, tax evasion and aggressive tax planning. New tax policies aimed at increasing fairness and
transparency in EU tax systems have been implemented, international cooperation has been increased
and minimum standards have been drawn up, also in line with international developments, for
instance at OECD level41. The external coherence of the Fiscalis programme has always been
assessed positively. For instance, the final evaluation of Fiscalis 2020 found the programme to be
‘coherent and consistent with EU priorities and complement other funding programmes’.
Concerning the alignment between the programme and other initiatives, the objectives of Fiscalis
are aligned with the Union anti-fraud programme (UAFP, managed by OLAF). The two actions are
highly complementary, with minimal risk of duplication or overlapping. However, practical
cooperation and synergies were limited, which meant that the potential for increased coordination

➢ The synergies between the IT systems and collaborative actions are significant and widely

As discussed in the section above, the significant synergies between the two ‘pillars’ of the Fiscalis
programme, namely support to IT systems and collaborative actions, are evident. Collaborative
actions have a crucial role in supporting the development and, in some cases, operation of the systems.
The case of TNA is emblematic: besides supporting the development of this IT system, the Fiscalis
programme funds the TNA expert team, which brings together the system’s users and plays an
important role in how the system is developed and integrated into the activities of tax authorities.

virtually impossible for the Member States to allocate the human resources needed for this purpose

value in their own right, but act together to support the uniform implementation and uptake of
EU tax policy. Both these aspects are essential to achieving the objectives of the programme. In this

and are therefore highly internally coherent.

4.2. How did the EU intervention make a difference and to whom? (EU added value)
EU added value means the changes brought about by the Fiscalis programme which are additional to
those that could be reasonably expected from Member State action alone. Previous evaluations have
consistently found the programme’s EU added value to be high, based on its supporting – and often
catalytic – role in tax policy development and implementation. The final evaluation of Fiscalis 2020
highlighted the EU added value of all the main programme components, including the IT systems
(‘which are crucial to ensuring the availability and sharing of information’), the collaborative
activities (previously known as joint actions and which gave ‘the administrations unequalled
opportunities for cooperation, communication and networking’) and the training activities (which
‘helped national tax administrations better understand and implement EU tax legislation and its
related procedures in a more uniform manner’ and improved ‘‘officials’ ability to work with the IT
systems’).
As already discussed, the programme has made a difference, in the first instance, to the users of the
IT systems (EESs) that are supported from the programme’s budget. These include the national tax
administrations of the EU Member States, who use the various systems both to collect and exchange
data and information and (especially in the case of the de-centralised systems) to ensure the systems
are interoperable with the relevant national components. They also include economic operators, who
are direct or indirect users of many of the IT systems in question.
The collaborative, human competency-building and training activities under the Fiscalis
programme have also made a significant difference to the national tax administrations of participating
countries – including EU Member States and the third countries that signed an agreement to
participate in the Fiscalis programme. More indirectly, these activities can benefit economic operators
and even the wider public, to the extent that the programme activities can help to effectively and
efficiently implement EU policies and legislation that aim to reduce tax fraud, tax evasion and
aggressive tax planning.
The feedback from national tax administrations via the survey regarding the overall value added of
the Fiscalis programme is overwhelmingly positive. As shown in Figure 13 below, the majority of
respondents reported that, ‘to a great extent’, the programme builds trust and leads to convergence
between participating tax administrations; helps to apply EU rules more effectively, consistently and
uniformly; and means EU legislation is implemented more quickly than would be possible without
Fiscalis. Responses were a little more nuanced as regards the question of whether the programme

and international cooperation, particularly by developing and implementing IT systems like VIES,
and projects such as VAT in the Digital Age, both of which were mentioned by multiple respondents.

IT systems
The Fiscalis programme’s support for developing, maintaining and upgrading IT systems

number of areas, in many of which it is mandated by EU legislation.
The in-depth case studies on four IT systems (TNA, DAC6, VIES-on-the-web and EMCS) confirm

key enabler. An explicit counterfactual scenario was developed: how would EU tax administrations
and economic operators exchange the relevant data and comply with their obligations if there was no

that, in each case, without the Fiscalis programme funding, there would be higher costs and

use these systems.
Collaborative activities
Based on the feedback received from Member State tax administrations (via the survey and
interviews), the collaborative activities are the most widely and consistently appreciated of the
various types of Fiscalis-supported activities. 82% of survey respondents ‘fully agreed’ that the
collaborative activities contribute to the fight against tax fraud, tax evasion and aggressive tax

aspects of added value that specifically related to collaborative activities within the Fiscalis
programme:
- Improved implementation of EU law and policy goals: this was particularly evident in areas
like the DAC, ViDA and CESOP initiatives. Collaborative efforts reportedly help ensure that
rules across Member States are applied consistently and facilitate the practical application of
complex regulations.
- Improved cooperation and coordination: beyond simply implementing rules, collaborative
activities fostered a sense of shared purpose and improved coordination among national tax
administrations. This included sharing best practices, developing common strategies and
aligning national initiatives with EU frameworks. The improved communication and
coordination were seen as crucial for addressing complex, cross-border tax challenges.
- Increased efficiency and effectiveness: by working together, Member States could leverage
each other’s expertise and resources, leading to more efficient and effective outcomes.

Examples included bilateral projects and developing joint approaches to common challenges.
This collaborative approach was thought to maximise the impact of the programme and help
ensure that resources were used effectively.
Expert teams
Expert teams are a specific sub-type of collaborative actions that pool resources across Member
States. They are used primarily to support the development and implementation of digital taxation
systems. Due to their specific nature, they require dedicated grant agreements, and the long-term
commitment of the experts involved. Unlike other collaborative actions, the programme funds the
salary costs of the officials involved, with a view to enabling the extensive collaboration required.
At the end of 2024, there were five expert teams funded by the Fiscalis programme (two others were
finalised in 2021). Some, but not all, of these struggled with a certain lack of commitment and
ownership among participating countries (as noted in the 2023 APR), which led to a streamlining
exercise. Based on the information available in the 2024 APR, and on feedback from national tax
administrations, there appear to have been significant differences between the different expert
teams in terms of effectiveness and added value:
- The Managed IT Collaboration (MANITC V) expert team, which supported digital
collaboration activities, acting as a secretariat, has completed its task. Because of the above-
mentioned streamlining exercise, it was decided not to launch another iteration of the expert
team, but to consider transforming it into a project group.
- The Transaction Network Analysis (TNA) and Central Electronic System of Payment
Information (CESOP) expert teams are widely seen as success stories. The 2024 APR notes
that, ‘in the area of VAT, the ongoing work of the TNA expert team and the CESOP expert
team represented important added value in the fight against VAT fraud’.
- For the other two teams, they completed their tasks but were not highlighted as particular
success stories by any consultees. Again, based on the 2024 APR, the development of data
analysis tool and other solutions for enhanced use of the tax information (DATANA) expert
team completed the key aspect of its mandate in 2024. Following this, it was ‘decided that the
work of this expert team was successfully completed according to the plan and that there
would be no need for a prolongation’. The Visits to Member States Directive on
Administrative Cooperation (VISDAC) expert team, supporting Member States in the
effective implementation and functioning of the DAC, ‘completed all 27 visits to Member
States during 2023-2024’.
During the consultation, the national tax administrations that provided detailed comments on the
added value of the expert teams – in particular the CESOP team – emphasised the practical benefits
of expert team involvement, including access to specialised expertise, the opportunity to share
knowledge across borders and the role of the expert teams in developing and implementing IT systems
related to taxation.
Thus, overall, it appears that expert teams have the potential to add significant value, but this is
highly dependent on the specific context and relies, in particular, on whether a sufficient number
of Member States consider the topic a high enough priority to make the expert team work effectively.
44
The experience of TNA and CESOP suggests that this is more likely to be the case for expert teams
that directly support the development and/or application of a specific IT system.
Training activities
Survey responses from national tax administrations suggest that training activities do add value,
but not necessarily to the same extent for all Member States. It depends on the resources, priorities
and materials that are available at national level. 55% of respondents ‘fully agreed’ that the Fiscalis
programme’s human competency building / training activities contribute to the fight against tax fraud,
tax evasion and aggressive tax planning (compared with 82% for collaborative activities, and 73%
for IT systems). And 45% ‘fully agreed’ that the human competency building / training activities
correspond to the needs of EU tax administrations (compared to 73% for collaborative activities and
41% for IT systems). It should be noted that the remainder either ‘tended to agree’ or responded
neutrally. Not a single respondent disagreed with this statement regarding any of the activities or
systems.
The case study on the LMS found that, as a whole, the LMS is of high quality and adds significant
value at a reasonable cost. It improved awareness and uptake of EU training, particularly for training
coordinators who integrate courses into national curricula. However, some of its features (hosting and
LTI integration) are more valuable for smaller Member States, which may value the EU LMS due to
cost savings or enhanced functionality. Larger tax authorities with existing national training platforms
are less likely to benefit significantly.
➢ Likely impact of discontinuing the Fiscalis programme
Many Member States expressed concerns and believed that (hypothetically) discontinuing the
programme or reducing the available funding would have negative impacts. Several reported that they
rely heavily on the programme funding, and that reduced funding could lead to decreased
participation, prioritisation of certain activities (often digitalisation) and fewer physical meetings. It
could potentially hinder the effective implementation of EU taxation policy. Survey respondents were
also asked to estimate the extent to which they would still be able to participate in collaborative
activities if the Fiscalis programme funding to cover expenses was either reduced by 50% or
eliminated entirely. Under both scenarios, just over half of respondents believed that this would lead
to a major reduction in participation. The remainder expected a minor reduction, but a few
respondents thought that, without any funding, officials from their country would no longer be able
to participate in any collaborative actions at all, or would have to limit their participation to online-
only events (which can help save scarce resources, but are less likely to generate the ‘softer’ benefits
of the programme, in particular trust-building and networking effects)46.
Thus, the programme as a whole, as well as all of the types of systems and activities it funds, provide
high EU added value. The Fiscalis programme supports the implementation of EU taxation policy
and legislation, and encourages collaboration, coordination and information exchange between

4.3. Is the intervention still relevant? (Relevance)
To evaluate the (continued) relevance of the programme, the evaluation looked at two main aspects,
namely the alignment of the programme’s objectives to the needs and challenges of the EU in the

The Commission’s overall policy priorities in the area of taxation for the period covered by this
evaluation were set out in a number of documents, most importantly, the 2020 Action Plan for Fair

cooperation between tax authorities and with other authorities to combat VAT fraud, to
continue to address fiscal risks inherent in excise goods, and to tackle the fraud opportunities

interactivity, methods of tracking the progress of participants and use of modern educational
technologies), the CLEP training courses and workshops for newcomers, and CLEP training courses
on TNA and CESOP. On the other hand, some respondents acknowledged that they do not make
extensive use of the training offer, citing reasons such as the existence of high-quality national
training, language barriers and the fact that some material is not updated frequently enough.
The case study on the LMS provides further evidence of the relevance of this system, which was
launched in 2021 as a single repository for the training and capacity-building activities carried out
under the Fiscalis programme (and Customs programme). It was created primarily to address the
difficulty faced by tax administration staff in locating and accessing training materials. Its centralised,
searchable platform solved the problem of scattered resources and improved awareness and uptake
of EU training, particularly for training coordinators who integrate courses into national curricula.
While the LMS also offers hosting and LTI integration, this is less relevant for larger tax authorities
with existing national training platforms (though integrating LTI functionalities would help the
Commission track and understand engagement with the courses). Smaller Member States, however,
may find value in the EU LMS due to cost savings or better functionality. The platform could also
potentially host nationally developed training, benefiting administrations with limited training
capacity. Finally, the LMS serves as a central access point for CLEP training, thus making it more
visible.

5.
WHAT ARE THE CONCLUSIONS AND LESSONS LEARNED?
This chapter presents the key conclusions and lessons learned based on the findings outlined in the
preceding chapter. It discusses the evaluation findings and the potential link between the results
achieved and more long-term impacts.
While the findings are in line with previous evaluations, the emphasis is on the findings derived
from the specialised methodology applied to this appraisal exercise. This focused on in-depth
case studies of four of the 30 IT systems (i.e. TNA, DAC6,
VIES-on-the-web and EMCS), each
of which compared observable experiences and results with a hypothetical ‘counterfactual’ scenario
of what would have been expected without EU support. The evaluation also included a case study on
the LMS (a platform introduced in the current iteration of the programme for disseminating e-learning
courses and other training material produced for the programme) and a programme assessment that
used desk research, a survey and interviews to assess other aspects of the programme horizontally.
5.1. Main achievements and strengths of the Fiscalis programme
As with previous iterations, the 2021-2027 Fiscalis programme can be considered very successful
at this stage of the funding period. It has continued to adapt to the needs of stakeholders while being
delivered largely as planned, implementing EU policy and generating real benefits and savings. The
programme’s main achievements and strengths can be summarised in terms of the four key
conclusions listed below. Each one is supported by specific examples from the case studies, which
accounted for a large part of the data and evidence collected for the evaluation.
The Fiscalis programme continued to be sufficiently adaptable to remain in line with
stakeholders’ needs and the wider policy environment
The programme’s design ensures that both its objectives and the actions selected are driven by the
policies it exists to support. The programme is first and foremost aligned with EU tax policy, but
since this is closely coordinated with wider policies and initiatives (e.g. the green transition, EU
enlargement, recovery from the pandemic and structural reforms), the programme is also broadly
consistent with other EU policies. Examples of complementarity were found in particular with the
Customs programme, which is jointly managed by DG TAXUD, as well as the RRF, the closely
related TSI (both managed by SG REFORM) and the cross-cutting European Green Deal. The
evidence collected as part of the evaluation also shows that this alignment is not only conceptual but
rooted in the wide variety of actions that launched to address specific needs, and in the fitness for
purpose of the programme’s main components: EESs, collaborative actions and capacity building.
The Fiscalis programme continues to be successful in implementing its activities and
delivering on its objectives
The design of the Fiscalis programme is needs-based and flexible, with practical responsibilities
allocated according to operational needs. This has allowed the programme to successfully deliver a
very wide range of activities, from complex IT projects, to a large number of structured and ad hoc
50
collaborative actions, to the development and roll-out of common training material. Achievements
and impacts vary depending on the nature and scale of specific funded actions. However, from a
delivery perspective, the programme has met or exceeded initial expectations/targets in all areas, and
stakeholder perceptions of the programme and its activities are overwhelmingly positive. With regard
to the four systems examined in the case studies, successful implementation has allowed tax
authorities and (where relevant) economic operators to interact in a secure and reliable manner. The
LMS has also been launched and is operating to a high standard.
The Fiscalis programme actions mutually reinforce each other and contribute significantly
to achieving the programme objectives
All three of the programme’s main action ‘types’ were found to be making significant contributions
to the specific objectives of coherent tax policy and implementation of EU tax law; fostering of
operational cooperation among tax authorities; and improved administrative capacity of tax
authorities. This was demonstrated by the general feedback from national administrations, by the
programme monitoring data, and by the findings of the case studies on specific IT systems and the
LMS. These achievements in turn contributed towards the programme’s general objectives (though
there are many other factors at play). The evaluation showed that the programme’s impact depended
not only on the quality and outputs of individual actions, but on the ways they work together and feed
off each other to produce the desired outcomes. As a result, although simply considering the
programme budget would suggest that most of its added value comes from the IT systems, in fact the
added value is generated by the combined effects of all types of actions. This is particularly true of
the role played by collaborative actions in developing and ensuring the proper use of funded IT
systems. Such actions include, in some cases, expert teams, which involve particularly extensive
cooperation between participating officials to achieve a common goal.
The Fiscalis programme continues to generate benefits that far outweigh the costs
Since the benefits and costs of the programme are highly specific to the action in question, this aspect
was examined mainly based on the in-depth case studies. In different ways and depending on their
functions and of tax policy area, the four IT systems examined were found to generate significant
tangible benefits and cost savings for tax authorities, for the European Commission and – where
relevant, such as when they use IT systems for compliance purposes – for economic operators. These
included efficiency gains from digitalising/automating tasks that were previously analogue,
increased productivity from being able to share more and better information seamlessly, reduced
waiting times due to the instantaneous availability of information, and direct and indirect effects on
reducing fraud. The counterfactual analyses generally showed that pooling resources to develop the
systems at EU level led to systems that were better at fulfilling their functions. They were also more
cost-effective than those that could have been achieved by the Member States on their own. As
mentioned above, the collaborative actions and capacity-building activities contributed in part by
helping to create the environment needed for the IT systems to function and be used as
envisaged, as well as by ensuring a common understanding and implementation of EU tax legislation.
51
Their relatively low cost was seen as a small price to pay given the leverage generated in terms of
increasing the effectiveness of the IT systems and giving tax authorities the means to work together.
5.2. Lessons learned and areas for improvement
As detailed above, Fiscalis is a highly relevant programme that has generated significant value over
the years, based on its sound overall design and its ability to adapt and improve incrementally. In that
spirit, while the evaluation has not found that major changes are needed, this section outlines areas
and aspects that could be improved, along with potential solutions that could be considered for the
remainder of the funding period and beyond.
The Fiscalis programme successfully supports the overall EU tax policy. However, the
multifaceted policy and political context within which it operates is not always conducive to
the most effective or efficient course of action
As commented, the evaluation shows how the programme contributes effectively to supporting EU
tax policy and ensures that the activities pursued under the programme correspond to real needs.
However, the surrounding context is complex and sometimes not conducive to the course of action
that would be the most effective or efficient. This is felt most strongly with the IT systems, for which
the advantages of centralised solutions from an operational and cost-effectiveness perspective
need to be balanced with issues such as existing legacy infrastructure and national-level
priorities. In the field of training, a similar situation was observed for the LMS, which is a high-
quality platform that has not yet realised its full potential (because most Member States still run e-
learning courses from their own LMSs rather than the EU one).
External factors will always affect the programme’s room for manoeuvre and cannot be simply
discounted. When it comes to deciding on which IT solutions to pursue, it has always been difficult
to assess costs and benefits robustly. This hampers efforts to assess the pros and cons of different
options. Against this backdrop, the approach pursued in analysing IT case studies did lead to more
concrete evidence than was previously available of the costs and benefits of several systems. They
were compared in each case to a plausible alternative. A similar approach could be used in the future,
either to inform potential changes to existing systems, or to consider the options for new systems.
Such assessments are time-consuming, and in some cases the option with the best cost-benefit ratio
may not be feasible for any number of reasons. However, such an approach would still more than pay
for itself if it led to more informed decision-making for large-scale IT projects.
The Fiscalis programme is fully coherent with a range of other Commission initiatives in
terms of alignment of objectives and complementarity of activities and outputs. Concrete
links with other initiatives continue to be limited
The evaluation found the Fiscalis programme to be fully coherent with a range of other Commission
initiatives in terms of alignment of objectives and complementarity of activities and outputs.
However, this was not the case for others, namely the Hercule component of the UAFP (managed by
OLAF), for which a recommendation in the previous evaluation proposed introducing a mechanism
52
The Fiscalis programme effectively combines different types of activities for pursuing
the desired objectives. Overcoming some of the persisting shortcomings in
communication, awareness and visibility could further boost the overall success of the
programme in the future
for coordinating with the Fiscalis programme, the single market programme and the IPA/TAIEX (DG
NEAR).
While the initiatives examined showed little risk of overlap with the Fiscalis programme and scope
for mutual reinforcement even in the absence of practical coordination, there may be missed
opportunities for identifying and exploiting synergies. The evaluation’s focus on IT systems meant
that these opportunities were not explored in detail. For this reason, it was also unclear why closer
collaboration with Hercule had not occurred, making it hard to understand whether and to what extent
this was considered a problem by programme stakeholders. The starting point for addressing the issue
is thus to decide whether it is in fact a problem, or whether the present situation of ‘passive coherence’
with certain other initiatives is sufficient. If it is a problem, then action towards establishing
coordination mechanisms should be pursued.
The different types of activities funded by the Fiscalis programme are closely linked and, as argued
above, work together to achieve the desired aims. However, while it is common knowledge that the
programme’s IT systems are supported by EU funding, some people are still unaware that these
activities form part of the Fiscalis programme. This limits information and data sharing among
stakeholders working on tax issues from different perspectives, and may lead to missed
opportunities, for example if IT staff do not know how to seek out support via collaborative actions.
It also leads to a narrow perception of the programme’s added value, meaning that its role in
implementing EU policy is not fully grasped. The APRs and other material produced on the
programme cover both IT aspects and collaborative and capacity-building actions, but these do not
seem widely read among national administrations.
In the short term, awareness of the role of the IT systems in the programme could be addressed
through more consistent branding. This would not require significant resources, but rather would
entail relatively simple efforts such as mentioning in the literature and interfaces of the systems that
they are funded by the Fiscalis programme and, where relevant, mentioning the link with other funded
actions. Similarly, NFCs could be asked to make a renewed effort to promote the programme brand
among users of the IT systems and other national officials, and the Commission could provide support
by offering guidance and other basic material as needed, emphasising the complementary role of
different types of actions. The e-learning courses on certain systems could also be used to promote
the fact that the systems form an integral part of the Fiscalis programme. Over time, this would create
a stronger association between the different strands of funded activities and increase the
visibility of the programme.
The programme’s revised grant management system has proven to be effective and to
function well despite the persisting differences in the level of experience and administrative
capacity. This may call for some adjusting in the future
53
The current programming period has seen a new approach to administering the collaborative actions,
which is the result of the compulsory new approach for grants across all Commission
programmes (including but not limited to the Fiscalis programme). This approach has been applied
since 2021 and involves electronically managing grants (with a new IT system, eGrants) and using a
new model grant agreement. This requires beneficiaries to be organised within a consortium, with the
grant coordinator becoming the single point of contact with the Commission for payments/recoveries.
Compared to the previous approach, whereby the Commission disbursed funding directly to each of
the beneficiaries, this represents a big change. The Member States responsible for the main
collaborative action grant, and the separate grants for individual expert teams, now have
considerably more administrative responsibility than in the past. Overall, the system has worked
well, but levels of experience and capacity differ, which has led to some teething problems.
To supplement the material and guidance on grant management already made available by the
Commission, national administrations could be encouraged to identify and share best practices
among themselves. A forum for this could be found within an existing collaborative action, or a
dedicated grant management collaborative action could be set up. This would ensure that successful
strategies are widely applied and help grants to run more smoothly in the future. It would
prevent Member States being discouraged from engaging with the programme due to administrative
constraints.
The new MEF for the Fiscalis programme is more manageable and purposeful than its
predecessor. However, there is scope to further simplify and streamline the overall process
of monitoring
Compared to its predecessor, the new MEF, introduced for the current programming period, has
reduced the number of indicators and simplified data collection and reporting structures, with a view
to establishing a more manageable and purposeful framework. The new MEF is clearly a step in the
right direction, but challenges persist, including some that were also experienced with the
previous MEF, such as an excessive number of indicators, burdensome processes for national
authorities and the Commission, and sometimes the usefulness of the reports and analysis produced.
A potential starting point for any changes could be to recognise that the diversity of actions and their
desired outputs and outcomes limits the amount of insight that can be gleaned from the most readily
quantifiable metrics. This should serve as a natural limit to the ambitiousness of the programme’s
MEF. Ideas for potential improvements include (1) minimising the amount of primary data to be
collected, which would help address ‘consultation fatigue’ among national coordinators and other
stakeholders; (2) further exploiting existing data to establish more informative indicators; and
(3) reducing the number of indicators, particularly at an output level where there is often low
correlation with programme performance and which is difficult to compare between actions.
The new LMS supporting the programme is cost-effective. Incremental improvements could
enhance further its effectiveness in serving training needs in the field of taxation
54
The evaluation assessed that, as a whole, the LMS platform is of high quality and adds significant
value at reasonable cost. While the findings were broadly positive, it was also noted that there are
some areas for incremental improvement, which could be addressed in the short- to medium-term
to improve the effectiveness of the LMS.
The findings suggest that the design and functionality of the LMS could be improved in terms of
the search function, more personalisation for logged-in users and introducing more language versions
(since the LMS site is currently only available in English)51. Integrating relevant training material
from national administrations and other organisations could also increase the LMS offering
while simultaneously making such material available to a wider audience. The limited uptake of the
LTI functionality has been a problem because it is needed to realise the full potential of the LMS,
particularly when it comes to tracking the engagement of users. Stakeholders attributed their
reluctance to use the functionality to compatibility and security issues, but in fact the LMS software
addresses both aspects. This suggests that the bottleneck is more about tax administrations
needing information and reassurance. Concentrated communication efforts could also boost
usage of the LMS and enhance its role as a centre of knowledge. Finally, some stakeholders
expressed confusion as to why CLEP events are organised on the LMS, while other capacity-building
activities follow a different procedure. Action should therefore be taken either to (1) limit the LMS
to being a platform for e-learning material or (2) to make the LMS the location for all capacity-
building actions funded by the programme.

request of Member States (approx. 1 100 localisations are available in LMS).

ANNEX II. METHODOLOGY AND ANALYTICAL MODELS USED
1. Approach
The interim evaluation of the Fiscalis programme mainly builds on the findings of an external study
conducted by a contractor during the period June 2024 – June 2025. The appraisal of the programme
over the period 2021-2024 relied on an overall approach that consisted of assessing the relevance,
effectiveness, efficiency, coherence and EU added value of the Fiscalis programme. To ensure that
the assessment was robust, the structured approach depended on an elaborated intervention logic,
operationalised evaluation matrix and a mix of data collection and analytical methods. The overall
approach included the following three main tasks:
-
structuring and scoping,
-
data collection,
-
analysis and lesson learned.
In line with the Commission’s Better Regulation Guidelines53, the evaluation criteria of relevance,
effectiveness, efficiency, coherence and EU added value were covered. They were addressed through
15 key evaluation questions:
1. What are the quantitative and qualitative effects of the programme?
2. How and to what extent have the IT systems for taxation funded by the programme contributed to
achieving of the general and specific programme objectives?
3. How and to what extent did the general collaborative activities, expert teams, the human competency-
building activities, and any other relevant activities contribute to achieving the programme’s objectives?
4. To what extent is the programme effective in communicating on and in disseminating its opportunities
as well as achievements?
5. To what extent is the MEF fit for purpose and suitable for providing information on progress towards
achieving the objectives of the programme? How can it be improved and simplified?
6. What are the costs and benefits of the EESs financed by the Fiscalis programme for different
stakeholders, including the Commission services? To what extent is the programme’s funding of the
common components of the EESs cost-effective?
7. To what extent are the other (non-EES) activities financed by the programme cost-effective? In
particular, how efficient are the training activities (including the use of the learning management
system/platform, the e-learning and relayed activities and the common learning events)?
8. Overall, how efficient is the governance of the programme during the period considered?
9. Have the objectives of the programme remained in line with single market needs, and with EU policy
needs and priorities?
10. Is the programme’s support for the common components of the EESs fit for purpose? If not, what
adjustments can be made, both during the current programming cycle and post-2027?

59
11. Is the programme’s support for collaborative activities, training, and other actions fit for purpose? If
not, what adjustments can be made under the current programming cycle (2021-2027)?
12. To what extent is the programme coherent with other EU initiatives/programmes with similar
objectives?
13. To what extent are the actions funded by the programme internally consistent?
14. What is the EU added value of the different types of activities funded under the Fiscalis programme?
15. Overall, what is the EU added value of the Fiscalis programme?
These questions were put into operation, and associated indicators and judgement criteria were
developed, to provide a framework for collecting data and making evaluative judgements (see Annex
III).
The approach to this exercise was informed by five main considerations. Firstly, the evolution of the
Fiscalis programme since 1998 – and the fact that its various iterations have been subjected to periodic
evaluations ever since – allows targeted analysis of specific components, without necessitating
another complete assessment. Secondly, the significant investment in IT systems requires a
comprehensive understanding of their effectiveness. Thirdly, the extensive coverage of
collaborative activities and capacity building in past evaluations and regular monitoring activities
has led to ‘consultation fatigue’ among stakeholders (meaning that additional consultation should be
targeted and limited to what is truly necessary). Fourthly, previous evaluations encountered
difficulties in measuring the costs and benefits of complex IT systems due to limited data. Lastly,
the recently introduced MEF offers more data and insight into the programme than was available
for previous evaluations.
2. Overall methodological framework
The methodological approach was characterised by a heavy reliance on case studies. This allowed
key issues that are of specific interest to be investigated in depth, while minimising the assessment of
the overall programme, already covered comprehensively in previous evaluations.

the three main tasks as listed above. The chosen data collection methods aimed to maximise cost
effectiveness, minimise duplication with existing information, target relevant stakeholders in a way
that limits their burden and avoids ‘consultation fatigue’, and generate the evidence needed to address
the evaluation questions, in particular as regards the use, results, costs and benefits of the IT systems.
