Structuring and scoping
The analytical framework initially drawn up was supplemented by desk research reviewing existing
programme documentation, annual progress reports and policy documents. An evaluation matrix was
aligned with the Fiscalis programme intervention logic to establish clear indicators, data sources and
judgement criteria for each evaluation question. The evaluation matrix (Annex III) addressed 15
questions and sub-questions, focusing on the programme’s effectiveness, efficiency, relevance,
coherence and EU added value. This task also involved developing the methodology, which included
establishing the sample of four EESs and the LMS for in-depth case studies and the data collection
strategy, both of which are described in more detail below.
The most extensive and important feature of the methodology for this evaluation was the case
studies on four EESs, which were carried out to allow an in-depth assessment of the aspect that
absorbs most of the Fiscalis programme funding (namely the IT systems). Rather than aiming to cover
a representative sample of the approximately 30 EESs, the case studies sought, for several different
types of systems54, to go into more depth than has been possible in the past and thereby shed new
light on the costs and benefits, and the factors promoting and hindering success. Previous evaluations
found it very difficult to provide quantified estimates of the costs and benefits of the IT systems (and
of the Fiscalis programme support for them), partly because the point of comparison against which
such costs and benefits should be assessed is not always clear. This is due, among other things, to the
54 The sample was chosen with a view to covering a range of approaches to IT systems (namely centralised vs decentralised), the
different types of taxation (direct, indirect and excise) and both long-established systems and systems that had been recently
introduced.
61
fact that IT systems typically go hand-in-hand with EU legislation that makes digital data exchange
mandatory. Therefore one cannot always simply assume that the absence of (the common components
of) the EESs would mean a return to the previous situation of mostly paper-based exchange of
information. To address this issue, a novelty for this evaluation was to compare each system to a
hypothetical ‘counterfactual’ scenario of what may have been expected in the absence of EU funding.
The only ‘non-IT’ case study – on LMS – served to examine an aspect of the programme that was
new for the current funding period. The programme assessment, rather than covering all remaining
actions in detail, was a limited exercise aimed at confirming the validity of previous evaluations and
gathering new insight into issues of particular interest, most importantly the EU added value of the
collaborative actions and expert teams.
Data collection and analysis
Existing documentation such as policy and programming documents, the Fiscalis programme APRs
and MEF data were reviewed to provide foundational understanding and context. Key information
and gaps were systematically mapped to guide further data collection steps. Data for both the case
studies and the programme assessment were collected via three main methods:
1. desk research to review a wide range of relevant sources of secondary data and information;
2. interviews with representatives of national tax authorities, the Commission and, where
relevant, economic operators and external contractors (in total 84 interviews were carried out,
in addition to ad hoc interactions with key Commission stakeholders);
3. three separate targeted surveys: a survey of NFCs in the national tax authorities of
participating countries (27 responses), online user surveys as part of two of the case studies
(on VoW, 1 248 responses) and the LMS survey (62 responses).
Overall, the evaluation sought to collect both qualitative and quantitative data, and data on both the
implementation of the programme and its impact.
Case studies on EESs
The selected case studies, VoW and TNA (indirect taxation), EMCS (excise duties) and DAC6 (direct
taxation), were chosen to ensure diversity in terms of system type, policy significance and age. The
evaluation aimed to assess the effectiveness, efficiency, relevance and EU added value of these
systems while providing detailed cost-benefit analyses.
To conduct the case studies, a specialised methodology was employed, comprising comprehensive
desk research and up to 20 in-depth stakeholder interviews per case study (Annex V). These
interviews included national tax authorities, EU officials, and system users across Member States,
providing a diverse and rich set of perspectives. The research focused on reviewing technical and
operational documents, fiscal performance data and existing policy documents. Triangulation of these
data sources ensured the consistency and validity of the findings.
The evaluation also involved constructing ‘counterfactual’ scenarios to better assess the impact of the
systems, by comparing the actual costs and benefits they generate with a hypothetical alternative
situation where no Fiscalis programme (or other EU) funding is available for developing and
62
maintaining the systems in question. Two main types of counterfactual situation were considered,
with the most appropriate one for each case study chosen as a point of comparison:
• One potential counterfactual scenario was a hypothetical continuation of the prevailing
situation before the system in question became operational, allowing a simple ‘before and
after’ comparison. However, this counterfactual scenario was not always appropriate as 1) certain
systems have been in use for over 20 years, making a return to paper-based information exchange
unlikely, and 2) many systems serve to address specific, legally mandated requirements within
EU legislation, meaning that a scenario where they simply did not exist would be unrealistic, as
it would not take into account the obligation for the various parties (including the Member States)
to comply with the relevant legal requirements to facilitate the electronic exchange of data.
• The other counterfactual scenario considered was to assume that Member States would still
need to meet the relevant legal obligations, but do so without EU support – in particular,
without the Fiscalis programme funding for common systems, components and/or technical
specifications. In other words, the Member States would have to find ways to ensure the relevant

Non-IT case study
In addition to the four case studies on EESs, the evaluation included a dedicated case study on the
LMS. The LMS (officially called the Customs & Tax EU Learning Portal)55, was launched in May
2021 as a one-stop shop for all training and capacity-building activities carried out under the Fiscalis
and Customs programmes. The LMS portal grants access to e-learning courses, webinars, nano-
learning modules, and e-books, of which some are restricted to customs and tax officials while others
are also open to other interested stakeholders (e.g. economic operators and academics). It also acts as
the centralised access point to Common Event Learning Programme (CLEP) trainings, allowing
national officials to present their applications for participating in online or in-person events.
This case study did not evaluate the content of the e-learning materials or the CLEP trainings, as that
had already been thoroughly analysed in previous assessments, and the findings remained applicable.
Instead, the case study concentrated on the LMS as a platform. It examined how well the platform
meets the needs and expectations of Member States, identified areas for functional improvement, and
assessed its complementarity with other national and international initiatives. Additionally, the case
study has a forward-looking element, aiming to explore potential changes that could enhance its value
for Member States. To achieve this, it investigated possible new features that might benefit the
Member States and assessed how receptive they were to broadening the LMS’s role to include hosting
national training modules in addition to European ones.

business case for the LMS, tender specifications and contracts for its development and operation, and
budgetary data. It also included the LMS platform itself and the training catalogue. Additionally,

Programme assessment
The five case studies were complemented by a broader programme assessment which aimed to gather
evidence on the Fiscalis programme as a whole and validate and to update the findings of the previous
Fiscalis programme evaluations. The analysis covers all evaluation criteria, with particular attention
to the EU added value, with the purpose of gathering any evidence indicating what the consequences
of discontinuing support to certain actions would be.
Data collection for the programme assessment focused on three elements: the desk review of a variety
of documents and sources of information (including the updated MEF, the Fiscalis programming
documents, previous evaluations and assessments, as well as other documentation monitoring the
programme (e.g. annual progress reports – APR)); an online survey of national Fiscalis coordinators;
and 14 interviews with EU and national-level counterparts, as well as exchanges with key DG
TAXUD stakeholders.
Final analysis and lessons learned
Part of the extensive analysis of both quantitative and qualitative data collected throughout the
programme was carried out by using statistical software for survey responses and programme
indicators to identify trends, correlations, and impact metrics. This included cost-benefit analyses (to
the extent possible, see discussion of limitations below) derived from the case studies. Qualitative
data were processed using coding techniques to reveal themes and patterns within interview
transcripts and survey responses. Triangulating data across multiple sources ensured the reliability
and consistency of conclusions.
The conclusions drawn from this comprehensive analysis addressed the five required evaluation
criteria of effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, coherence, and EU added value. These highlighted the
achievements of the Fiscalis programme while also pinpointing areas for improvement, supported by
robust evidence. A stakeholder workshop was also organised by the contractor carrying out the
external supporting study to validate the preliminary conclusions and incorporate additional feedback
from representatives of Member State tax authorities, aiding in the refinement and completion of the
analysis.
Additionally, the analysis phase identified lessons learned, best practices, and areas for potential
improvement. These lessons are deemed relevant for enhancing future programming decisions and
increasing the programme’s overall impact and efficiency.
3. Limits to the evidence base and robustness of findings
Rather than aiming to cover a representative sample of the approximately 30 EESs, the case studies
sought, for several different types of system57, to go into more depth than has been possible in the
past, and thereby shed new light on the costs and benefits, and factors promoting and hindering
success. Previous evaluations found it very difficult to provide quantified estimates of the costs and
57 The sample was chosen in conjunction with DG TAXUD with a view to covering a range of the types of approaches to
IT systems (namely centralised vs decentralised), the different types of taxation (direct, indirect and excise), and both
long-established systems and systems that had been recently introduced.
66
benefits of the IT systems (and of the Fiscalis programme support for them), partly because the point
of comparison against which such costs and benefits should be assessed it is not always clear. One
reason for this is that IT systems typically go hand-in-hand with EU legislation that makes digital
data exchange mandatory, and so one cannot always simply assume that the absence of (the common
components of) the EES would imply a return to the previous situation of mostly paper-based
exchange of information. To address this issue, a new feature of this evaluation was to compare each
system to a hypothetical ‘counterfactual’ scenario – agreed with DG TAXUD – of what may have
been expected in the absence of EU funding.
The only ‘non-IT’ case study – which looked at the LMS – served to examine an aspect of the
programme that was new for the current funding period. The programme assessment, rather than
covering all remaining actions in detail, was a limited exercise aimed at confirming the validity of
previous evaluations and gathering new insight into issues of particular interest to DG TAXUD, most
importantly the EU added value of the collaborative actions and expert teams.
Overall, the methodology proved effective. The counterfactual approach to the case studies on EESs,
harvested insights of a different nature and scale than had been previously achieved, by pinpointing
the ways in which EESs – together with related collaborative actions – affect the work of national
administrations and economic operators and generate EU added value, compared to the most likely
alternative scenario. With some minor exceptions, it was possible to identify and engage with
stakeholders as hoped, ensuring that the case studies were able to build a solid evidence base. The
LMS case study and programme assessment were also implemented largely as planned and obtained
the expected input. That said, there are two key limitations that should be pointed out:
▪ Trade-off between depth and breadth: based on the considerations set out above, the
evaluation deliberately chose to go into more depth on specific IT systems, which necessarily
meant that other IT systems and aspects of the programme, particularly the collaborative
actions, could not be assessed in as much detail as for previous evaluations. For this reason,
the evidence for certain evaluation questions (particularly those not focused on the EESs) was
limited. In these cases, key findings and conclusions from previous evaluations were used as
a starting point, and either confirmed, refuted, or built on, based on the available data and
information.
▪ Fragmented IT cost data: the rationale for the approach based on in-depth IT case studies
was to include a detailed ‘cost-accounting’ exercise on the systems being studied. As part of
this, the study involved IT cost-accounting experts on the team, and developed a detailed
framework for EU-level costs in agreement with DG TAXUD. However a reduced data set
was available, covering fewer cost categories and a shorter timeframe than initially planned.
For this reason, while the IT case studies were able to generate significant and – in many
instances, quantitative – insight, it was not possible to conduct the full cost-accounting
exercise initially planned.

Summary response to evaluation questions on EFFICIENCY
The evaluation identified multiple benefits that the four EESs have brought to tax authorities and
economic operators. Process automation has led to notable efficiency gains, allowing tax
administrations both to save and to redirect resources from routine tasks to more productive,
strategic roles like fraud detection. Additionally, these systems have yielded several indirect
impacts such as fraud deterrence and a reduction in waiting times, which improves commercial
activity and protects the EU’s tax revenues. Economic operators also benefit from substantial
savings in resource allocation and VAT verification costs, particularly with VoW and EMCS.
Despite these successes, there remain areas for improvement. Enhancing the user-friendliness of
the systems and considering greater centralisation could deliver further efficiencies, although any
changes has to be analysed against the sensitivity of information and political priorities. There are
several other specific suggestions for simplification for each case study including: expanding TNA
data sources, using AI to increase efficiency, standardising data across Member States for VoW, and
addressing DAC6 manual input challenges in third countries. Overall, while the Fiscalis programme
has markedly improved the efficiency of the administration of and participation in the EU’s tax
regime, ongoing refinements and improvements could further optimise its impact.
It needs to be acknowledged that since this evaluation focused primarily on assessing (via in-depth
case studies) the effectiveness and efficiency of selected IT systems (EESs) supported by the Fiscalis
programme, it did not collect a very substantial amount of new evidence on the efficiency of other
(non-EES) activities. Nonetheless, the feedback collected and documentation reviewed confirm that
the conclusions in the final evaluation of Fiscalis 2020 programme on the efficiency of the non-EES
activities supported by the programme remain valid, namely that the collaborative and training
activities are broadly cost-effective. Their share of the overall Fiscalis programme’s budget is small,
but (as discussed under other evaluation questions) they add significant value by enabling national
tax administrations to work together and build their capacities and competencies on relevant topics
of interest; in many instances, they also support the effective and efficient development and
application of the EESs. In the absence of any major changes to the way collaborative and training
activities are implemented, there is therefore nothing to suggest the non-EES activities have become
any less efficient than under previous iterations of the Fiscalis programme.
In conclusion, the Fiscalis programme’s governance structure seems to be broadly efficient in
some respects with a relatively clear structure for decision-making as laid out in key documents.
However, stakeholders pointed out specific areas of improvement and the programme faces
challenges in terms of procedural complexity and transparency in decision-making. It remains to be
seen whether devolving responsibility for managing the collaborative actions to the Member States
will increase the efficiency of this aspect of the programme. Nevertheless, additions such as the
MASP-T framework have purportedly improved decision-making procedures and collaboration.

Summary response to evaluation questions on RELEVANCE
Since the relevance of the programme has been extensively assessed and substantiated by previous
evaluations, this evaluation focused on ascertaining the extent to which the conclusions of the
Fiscalis 2020 programme final evaluation are still valid. To briefly summarise, that evaluation
found that the underlying challenges and needs the programme aims to address were still present; that
the relevance of EESs in the daily operations of both tax authorities and economic operators was high
and growing; and that collaborative actions were also highly relevant.
Overall, there was no negative feedback from the stakeholders consulted in this study on the extent
to which the programme responds to EU policy needs and priorities in the area of taxation, nor of any
shortcomings or areas of misalignment between the two. Some noted that the Fiscalis programme
design is sufficiently flexible to provide support to address any new or emerging priorities, and
especially to fund digital solutions that may be needed. This is evidenced, for example, by the creation
in 2010 of the Eurofisc Network to combat cross-border VAT fraud in the EU and its continued
operation and evolution since then (supported by the Fiscalis programme via several project groups).
This includes its use since 2019 of the Transaction Network Analysis (TNA) electronic system, which
was also developed with programme funding. For details, see the case study on TNA.
On the IT systems specifically (i.e. the common components of the EESs), which is the focus of this
evaluation question, 86% of respondents agreed (almost half of them ‘fully’) that these correspond to
their needs. The remaining 14% gave a neutral response; none disagreed. This confirms that, overall,
the programme’s support for the common components of the EESs is fit for purpose; however,
the fact that the responses are less ‘enthusiastic’ than for the collaborative actions suggests that there
may be scope for some improvements in the way they are delivered, or that awareness of the
programme’s role in the EESs is still limited.
According to the national tax authorities that responded to the survey (see Annex V), the
collaborative actions correspond very closely to their needs. Nearly all respondents agreed with this
statement, and over 70% agreed ‘fully’. Some respondents explained that collaborative actions have
positive impacts on tax administrations, and that without them there would be a higher risk of
misalignment with EU legislation and less tax harmonisation across the EU. On the human
competency-building / training actions, again a clear majority (86%) of respondents agreed (a little
over half of them ‘fully’) that these correspond to the needs of EU tax administrations (with the
remainder giving a neutral response). This confirms such actions are also fit for purpose, although
perhaps not to the same extent as the collaborative actions referred to above. Competency-building
actions that were highlighted as especially well aligned with needs included the e-learning courses
(described by one respondent as ‘excellent’ in terms of completeness and depth, interactivity, ways

Summary response to evaluation questions on EU ADDED VALUE
The survey feedback provided by national tax administrations on the overall added value of the
Fiscalis programme is overwhelmingly positive. The majority of respondents reported that the
programme builds trust and leads to convergence between participating tax administrations, that it
helps to apply EU rules more effectively, consistently and uniformly, and that it means EU legislation
is implemented more quickly than would be possible without the Fiscalis programme ‘to a great
extent’. A little more nuanced were responses to the question of whether the programme adds value
above and beyond initiatives at national level, without any duplication and overlap; even so, over
90% of respondents believed it does so to a greater or lesser extent. In response to follow-up
questions, respondents reported that the Fiscalis programme has had a significant impact on efficiency
and international cooperation, particularly through the development and implementation of IT
systems like VIES and projects such as VAT in the Digital Age, both of which were mentioned by
multiple respondents.
The conclusions of the final evaluation of the Fiscalis 2020 programme are still fully valid. The
programme, as well as all of the types of systems and activities it funds (see the previous evaluation
question), provide high EU added value. The Fiscalis programme supports the implementation of
EU taxation policy and legislation, enabling collaboration, coordination and information exchange
between national tax administrations that is vital to the effective, efficient and consistent application
of the former, and thereby helps to enhance the functioning of the internal market, and pursue a variety
of taxation policy objectives as outlined above (see assessment of Relevance). Without the
programme, national tax administrations would essentially be left to their own devices when it comes
to implementing EU taxation policy rules and mechanisms, which would be highly likely to be
detrimental to all of the aspects outlined previously.

This section presents an analysis of the responses provided by Member States on experiences with

The initial input was gathered through a survey developed by the contractor performing the external
study and refined with feedback from DG TAXUD. The survey was launched on 8 November
2024and remained open beyond the original deadline of 6 December 2024, with 15 responses received
by 13 December. It covered 13 Member States and two other participating countries. While this earlier
86
survey formed the foundation for the consultation, it has since been complemented by follow-up
interviews. These interviews were carried out with national Fiscalis coordinators (NFCs) from seven
of the countries who had completed the questionnaire – allowing for deeper exploration of their
responses – as well as with stakeholders from seven Member States who had not participated in the
initial survey. The analysis presented in this section draws on both sources.
Visibility of the Fiscalis programme and dissemination of information
The focus of this section is on the visibility of the Fiscalis programme within tax administrations,
based on the insights provided though both the initial survey and the follow-up interviews.
According to the feedback collected, awareness of which IT systems are funded by the Fiscalis
programme was generally ‘moderate to low’ among tax officials. Nine participants indicated that
officials in their administration are aware ‘to some extent’, while eight described awareness as being
only ‘to a small extent’. A smaller group – four participants – described a higher level of awareness.
One participant was uncertain.
When asked about the broader visibility of the Fiscalis programme within their administrations,
several participants noted that awareness tends to be concentrated among senior management or
officials involved in international activities, while regular staff often have limited exposure. Some
administrations have internal structures or dedicated coordinators that help promote the programme,
but others reported gaps in communication and a lack of clarity about which initiatives are funded by
the Fiscalis programme. While a few participants did not view low awareness as problematic, others
suggested that better internal information sharing (such as brief statements, info sessions, or clearer
messaging) could strengthen engagement and improve the overall impact of the programme.
Awareness of collaborative actions funded by the Fiscalis programme tends to be higher among those
directly involved but still remains limited for those officials not engaged in these activities.
The next question was on sources of information about the Fiscalis programme. A key role is played
by NFCs: in fact, the majority of respondents highlight that dissemination activities by coordinators
are one of the main means to receive information on the programme. The PICS platform and direct
interaction with colleagues in their own administration were cited as frequent sources by over half of
respondents (respectively 15 and 20 out of 22), together with direct interaction with colleagues within
one’s own administration (12 out of 22). Other sources seem comparatively less important.

All in all, the moderate level of awareness reported within tax administration about the role of the

Programme management
The second section of the questionnaire and interviews focuses on management aspects, particularly
the effort and administrative burden required across different types of activities.
In general terms, most respondents (19 out of 22) find the overall administrative burden related to the
Fiscalis programme to be moderate or significant. Significantly, three respondents pointed out how
the change in programme management, with a shift of management responsibilities from the
Commission to participating countries, has significantly increased the administrative burden, which
is reportedly particularly challenging for smaller (and under-resourced) national administrations.
Issues with the registration process and key implementation challenges were explored in more depth
through follow-up questions. Respondents pointed out that registration remains more complex than
necessary, with overlapping systems (e.g. ART, CLEP, emails), manual steps, and a lack of
harmonisation. While some tools are still seen as helpful, most respondents expressed a clear desire
for simplification and better integration. More broadly, the financial aspect emerged as the most
88
significant concern. The rigid budget rules, requiring 80% of the budget to be spent before additional
funding can be requested, were frequently cited as a key obstacle. Combined with staffing shortages
and complex financial procedures, these factors have placed increasing pressure on national teams,
making it harder to plan and manage events effectively.
The survey then assessed more in detail the burden related to (i) collaborative activities (other
than expert teams), and (ii) expert teams. The tax administrations of 18 of the 22 interviewees had,
since the start of the current Fiscalis programme, initiated at least one collaborative action (not
including expert teams). Of those, nine said that the burden connected to initiating a collaborative
action was moderate, one that it was minor, and another eight that it was significant, but would not
discourage them from initiating other actions in future. Of the four administrations that did not initiate
any collaborative action over the period reviewed, one reported that the main reason for this was the
lack of human resources, while other two are non-EU participating countries.
The administrative effort required for long-term participation can be a significant motivating factor,
but the lack of human resources and time is often a key challenge. Tasks like selecting the appropriate
action policy and engaging relevant Member States can be complex, and many smaller
administrations struggle with the increased workload. Experts in these administrations are often
overwhelmed by their existing responsibilities, which limits their capacity to initiate or lead new the
Fiscalis programme activities. While some administrations, such as those hosting groups, can manage
specific tasks, they are not generally in a position to initiate large-scale events. Despite the
considerable administrative burden, the process can be managed effectively once personnel become
familiar with it, with the NFC playing a crucial role in guiding colleagues through the process.
The feedback is overall similar when it comes to participation as a member of the consortium for

this appears related to a lack of interest or specific expertise.
Finally, respondents were asked to compare the overall administrative burden under the current the
Fiscalis programme funding cycle with the arrangements of the previous cycle. Just over half of the
respondents (12 out of 22) believe that the current management process is more or much more
onerous than the previously, while another seven did not experience any change, and only three
reported improvements. Additionally, respondents noted that NPCs handle more responsibilities in
the current cycle, including budget management and reporting, which were previously managed by
the Commission. The introduction of the grant coordinator role has increased national coordinators’
independence but also created coordination challenges. As their role becomes more operational,
NPCs face a heavier workload with fewer resources.
Overall added value of the Fiscalis programme
The third section of the questionnaire focused on the extent to which respondents believe that the
programme has contributed to achieving results that could not have been achieved by national
administration acting on their own, i.e. generating EU added value. Most respondents find
collaborative actions useful or very useful (21 out of 22), while 20 out of 22 respondents find expert
teams useful, though they were slightly less enthusiastic on them than on collaborative actions.
Respondents specifically emphasised the significant value of collaborative actions and expert teams
in promoting cooperation, sharing best practices, and harmonising the implementation of EU laws.
In particular, the CESOP expert team was highlighted for its role in enabling countries to contribute
to and benefit from these efforts, fostering a unified approach to issues like fiscal fraud and VAT
90
implementation across the EU. These actions are seen as crucial for improving national
implementation processes and encouraging collaboration among tax administrations.
The feedback on the overall added value of the Fiscalis programme was also overwhelmingly
positive, with the majority of respondents finding that the Fiscalis programme contributed to a faster
implementation of EU legislation and application of EU rules. The area with the most positive
responses was the extent to which the Fiscalis programme contributed to building trust and to
convergence among tax administrations. However, there was some difference in opinion regarding
whether the Fiscalis programme adds value beyond national-level initiatives, with a few respondents
expressing uncertainty or differing views on this aspect.
Through follow-up questions, respondents reported that the Fiscalis programme has had a significant
impact on efficiency and international cooperation, particularly through the development and
implementation of IT systems like VIES and projects such as VAT in the Digital Age, both of which
were mentioned a couple of times. Additionally, respondents highlighted the value of workshops, IT
training, and collaborative networks, including those focused on e-invoicing, which have greatly
supported tax administrations in implementing EU legislation and sharing best practices.

Validation of and reflections on the previous evaluation
This final section of the survey investigated the extent to which the conclusions drawn in the final
evaluation of the Fiscalis 2020 programme (2014-2020) were still valid in the context of the current
Fiscalis programme (2021-2027).
The feedback provided by the 22 respondents suggests that the majority strongly agreed that the
impact of the Fiscalis programme was positive across various areas. Specifically, most respondents
highlighted the programme’s significant contribution to enhancing authorities’ administrative
capacity, the reduction of administrative burdens, and the fight against tax fraud, tax evasion, and
aggressive tax planning. While the consensus was overwhelmingly positive, some respondents were
neutral, particularly regarding the alignment of IT systems and collaborative actions with the specific
needs of EU tax administrations, which indicates some uncertainty.

3. Case study consultation activities
Each case study included the collection of documentary evidence and interviews with stakeholder
directly involved in the technical aspects of the Fiscalis EESs but also with policy officers. The
stakeholder consultations were adapted to each case study’s EES. Additionally, concise online user
surveys were conducted for two of the case studies, namely VoW and the LMS. More specifically for
each case study:
Transaction Network Analysis system (TNA)
Stakeholders consulted included representatives from DG TAXUD, as well as 15 Eurofisc liaison
officers, including (i) the Eurofisc chair and grant coordinator for the TNA expert team; (ii) the
current and former WF1 coordinators; (iii) the current WF2 coordinator; (iv) the Europol, EPPO and
OLAF contact point within Eurofisc; (v) other ENLOs and ELOs, including members of both WF1
and WF2, and members of the TNA expert team.

Consultations were conducted with Administrative Cooperation on Direct Taxation (ACDT)

administrations, covering both policy and operational dimensions of DAC6. These included
representatives of the competent authority responsible for implementation, IT specialists involved in
system development and management of the central directory, and coordinators or analysts supporting

VIES-on-the-web (VoW) system
In-depth interviews were conducted, each lasting around an hour, with officials of the tax
administrations (members of SCAC and SCIT – the standing committees on administrative

A short survey was launched on the VoW interface to assess the added value of the system, and of
the ability to check VAT numbers at the pan-European level compared to national interfaces (the
counterfactual scenario). This survey was designed to capture economic operators’ perspectives on
the costs and benefits of VoW. Access was provided through a link on the VoW website59, and the
survey ran for four weeks, from 10 March to 6 April 2025. The questionnaire clarified that VoW is
not a centralised database of VAT numbers but rather functions as an interface forwarding requests
to national VIES systems; the clarification was intended to prevent economic operators mistakenly
attributing blaming the VoW system for issues with national databases and their updates to the VIES.
A total of 1 248 survey responses were received. Most survey respondents were from Italy (21%),
Germany (10%), Poland (11%), and the Netherlands (7%), with the remaining respondents more or
less evenly distributed among the other 23 EU MS. Among the companies surveyed, 36% were micro
enterprises, 27% were small enterprises, 18% were medium enterprises, and 19% were large
enterprises.
In addition to the survey, six interviews were conducted. They were with a key business association
(one interview) as well as with specific member companies nominated by the association (three
interviews with medium and large enterprises in the retail, online platforms and energy sectors). Two
of the interviews were held with large companies, including a digital platform. This interview
approach complemented the survey and allowed for cross validation of survey results.

scheduled service downtimes, noting instances where planned downtimes were not announced or did

Several interviews were conducted to help build the evidence base of the case study. Multiple policy

industry associations from the alcohol and tobacco sectors. These stakeholders shared their views

Learning Management System (LMS)
For this case study, the stakeholder consultation consisted of two main parts:
• A series of interviews with DG TAXUD, the contractor responsible for developing and operating
the LMS, and tax officials taking part in the TSG from five Member States. The sample took into
account diversity in terms of both geography and varying levels of engagement with the LMS
based on the statistics provided by DG TAXUD, and covered Germany, Greece, Ireland,
Lithuania and Spain66. Eight interviews were conducted in total, based on a semi-structured
format that used pre-defined questions agreed with DG TAXUD, while also allowing interviewees
to go into more detail on issues of particular importance to them. While a few additional Member
States declined to participate due to limited experience with the LMS, the sample was sufficient
to gather significant insight into the LMS and in line with the approach originally proposed.
• A survey of LMS users was promoted on the LMS site itself as well as by TSG members. The
survey was conducted together with the parallel case study on the LMS for the Customs platform
and garnered 62 replies, of which 10 mentioned an interest in taxation only and 19 mentioned an
interest in both taxation and customs; the remaining 33 respondents expressed an interest in
customs only and are not referred to in this report. Of the respondents interested in tax, 15 were
from tax authorities and 10 from customs authorities, while two represented both tax and customs
administrations, and just two were from private organisations. Given the relatively small sample
size, and the fact that most respondents seem likely to have been TSG members rather than course
participants as such, the survey cannot be deemed representative of all LMS users, but it
nonetheless adds value by providing structured input on a wide range of issues of interest, thereby
serving to corroborate and expand on the interview findings. In addition, the case study also drew
on the findings of the survey and interviews conducted for the programme assessment part of the
evaluation, which included several questions on the LMS in addition to other topics.
Overall, the methodology was implemented as planned and collected sufficient insight for a robust
and meaningful analysis. A limitation that should be noted is that very little input was collected
directly from economic operators / private stakeholders, an important secondary target audience for
the LMS. In addition, no formal usage targets were set prior to the LMS launch, limiting the extent
to which it has been possible to gauge success in terms of initial expectations for the platform. Instead,
the findings have been contextualised based on the views and perceptions of stakeholders, and the
judgement of the evaluators, transparently explained.
